“Why is engineering hiring taking so long?”

START WITH THE OUTCOME

Make the question specific before opening a dashboard.

The sponsor wants predictable engineering interview progress. Recruiters need clear next steps; hiring managers need feasible interview and feedback expectations. Faster movement is a proposed goal, not permission to reduce assessment quality.

Working objective: identify avoidable stage delays, validate the baseline and agree ownership for a limited pilot.

FACILITATION CHOICE

Align the three perspectives.

Head of Talent: which business outcome matters, and which roles are in scope?

Recruiter: where does the next step wait, and what is recorded?

Hiring manager: which constraints can the team change, and who owns feedback?

Four questions I would ask

Open each question to reveal a fictional customer answer and how it changes the investigation.

1. What does “slow” mean, and where does the clock start?

Customer: “Mostly the engineering interview loop. We have been mixing application age with interview-stage time.”

Implication: agree stage entry and exit definitions. Measure completed-stage duration separately from active waiting time. The export cannot establish time-to-fill without requisition dates.

2. Is the data complete enough to support that conclusion?

Customer: “Some migrated applications have missing stage-entry timestamps.”

Implication: quantify excluded duration records and reconcile a sample with the ATS. A long-looking delay can reflect a timestamp problem.

3. Which other explanations should we investigate?

Customer: “Interviewer availability, delayed feedback and specialist role mix could all contribute.”

Implication: compare roles and teams, then review scheduling and feedback evidence. Stage duration alone does not establish which explanation is true.

4. Who can change the process, and what can we commit to?

Customer: “The TA lead owns the process, hiring managers allocate interview capacity and our CSM owns routine follow-up.”

Implication: propose a focused engagement with explicit responsibilities, acceptance criteria and a review date. Confirm availability before committing to delivery.

Decision boundary: this exercise evaluates workflow records and reporting definitions. It does not assess candidate suitability or recommend hiring decisions.

Next: explain what the evidence supports.
A FIVE-MINUTE CUSTOMER LESSON

Stage delay is a signal. Validate its meaning.

  1. Define the clock: calendar time between stage entry and exit; not interviewer effort.
  2. Separate populations: completed stages describe past movement. Active waits show unfinished work and need their own view.
  3. Inspect coverage: missing or inconsistent timestamps are excluded from durations, not silently treated as zero.
  4. Find a tractable action: review scheduling availability, feedback timestamps and next-step ownership before prescribing a fix.
  5. Check the pilot: use a comparable cohort and stable definitions. A change in the median is not proof that your intervention caused it.
WHAT I WOULD SAY ON A CUSTOMER CALL

“Let’s validate the clock before setting a target.”

“The case shows longer completed stages in one part of the engineering loop. That gives us a place to investigate. It does not yet tell us whether scheduling, feedback or data capture is responsible.”

“I’d reconcile a sample with you, agree ownership and pilot a change. We would then review both speed and completeness using the same definitions.”

Quality of Hire: unavailable here. It requires an agreed definition, appropriate post-hire evidence and an observation window; these stage records cannot establish it.

How would you respond?

The Head of Talent sees a longer stage median in October and says, “The interviewers are underperforming.”

Deliverables & acceptance

Days 1–3: discovery and validated baseline. Accept when source definitions, coverage and excluded records are documented.

Days 4–7: diagnosis and scoped pilot design. Accept when the sponsor and delivery owners confirm actions, responsibilities and measures.

Days 8–10: workflow playbook and enablement. Accept when the CSM and recruiting team can explain routine checks and escalation rules.

30-day review: assess pilot evidence and limitations. These timings are proposed and depend on customer availability.

Responsibilities & boundaries

Customer: authorised exports, source validation, stakeholder availability and approval of process changes.

Consultant: baseline, analysis, recommendations, teaching and a clear handover.

Excluded: ATS migration, integrations, bespoke software, individual hiring decisions and unsupported Quality of Hire conclusions.

Change request: clarify the need, estimate effort and ask the sponsor to approve a scope change before committing.

Privacy, responsible use & legal limits

CSV contents stay in this browser tab. Uploaded CSV contents are never sent to Supabase. The fictional demo dataset is loaded from Supabase, with a bundled fallback. Optional analytics, enabled only after your consent, record viewed sections, action names, active viewing time. Analytics contain no uploaded records, search terms, filenames or recommendation text. A random session ID lasts only for this page visit; your consent choice is stored locally for six months. Analytics events are deleted after 30 days. You can withdraw using Analytics settings. The application stores no IP address or IP network in analytics; infrastructure may still process connection metadata. Supabase and hosting providers may receive IP addresses in their operational logs. There are no AI API calls. Hosting and sign-in providers may process access logs independently. Reload or use Clear data to remove application data from this app; downloaded files and clipboard copies remain on your device.

Use opaque candidate and application IDs. The importer discards name, email, phone, CV, note and unrecognised columns before diagnostics. Role titles and stages become local references; source and rejection reason retain presence only. Duplicate checks use candidate ID plus role. IDs, dates and linked operational records can still identify people: this is pseudonymisation, not anonymisation. Prepare the export without unnecessary personal data before selecting it. Exported repair queues contain pseudonymous record references: protect them and apply your organisation’s retention policy.

For authorised recruiting operations staff only. This tool checks records; it does not assess, rank or select candidates, infer personal characteristics, or make employment decisions. AI review is an optional manual workflow. Counts below five are suppressed and other counts bucketed; review the remaining context before sharing. No candidate data is automatically sent to Le Chat. The optional brief contains operational totals only; never add individual candidate information to it.

This prototype is not certified GDPR or EU AI Act compliant. Your organisation must establish lawful basis, transparency, access controls and retention, assess processors and transfers, and decide whether a DPIA is required. Any future AI functionality that evaluates candidates requires a fresh legal and risk assessment. Read the safeguards and deployment checklist. Real hiring use needs an organisation-specific legal review covering the EU and relevant US jurisdictions.
